case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of high fever, cough productive of purulent, blood-streaked sputum, and shortness of breath for 2 days. One week ago she had abrupt fever, myalgias, headache, and dry cough, and a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for influenza A. She improved for 2 days and then worsened. She did not receive an influenza vaccine this season. Her temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Crackles are heard over both lungs. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) with 88% neutrophils. A chest x-ray shows patchy infiltrates in several lobes of both lungs with small thin-walled cavities. Sputum Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters, and culture grows coagulase-positive Staphylococcus aureus. The diagnosis is Staphylococcus aureus bronchopneumonia complicating influenza.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her recent influenza infection predisposed her to this bacterial pneumonia?
options: Consumption of serum complement by viral immune complexes
Necrosis of ciliated airway epithelium impairing clearance
Selective depletion of CD4+ T cells in bronchial lymphoid tissue
Suppression of IgA class switching in mucosal plasma cells
approach: Notice the timing: influenza, a brief improvement, then a new high fever with purulent sputum. This is the classic pattern of secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Influenza replicates in and kills ciliated columnar cells of the trachea and bronchi.
Without cilia, the mucociliary escalator stops working, so bacteria from the upper airway reach and colonize the lower airways.
questions.why: Influenza virus infects the ciliated epithelium of the respiratory tract and causes necrosis and desquamation of these cells. Loss of ciliary clearance lets inhaled or aspirated bacteria stay in the lower airways. Viral damage also exposes basement membrane and other attachment sites, and the virus temporarily dampens alveolar macrophage and neutrophil function. Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae are the classic secondary invaders, usually appearing several days into the illness or after brief improvement. Influenza A itself is a public health concern because avian and human strains can reassort in a shared host and produce a novel strain.
whyNot: Influenza does not cause clinically important complement depletion. Complement consumption by immune complexes is seen in disorders such as lupus and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Correct.

Selective CD4+ T-cell depletion is the hallmark of HIV infection. It predisposes to Pneumocystis and other opportunists, which is a different pattern from acute post-influenza staphylococcal pneumonia.
Influenza does not block IgA class switching. A primary failure of IgA production is selective IgA deficiency, an inherited disorder with recurrent sinopulmonary infections over years.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms also characteristically causes this pattern of lung involvement?
options: Coxiella burnetii
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Chlamydophila pneumoniae
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
approach: Classify the pattern first: patchy infiltrates scattered through several lobes of both lungs fit bronchopneumonia, which is centered on bronchioles.
Lobar pneumonia fills an entire lobe uniformly, and atypical pneumonia is interstitial.
Match the pattern to organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa classically cause bronchopneumonia.
questions.why: Bronchopneumonia begins in the bronchioles and spreads to the surrounding alveoli. The result is patchy foci of neutrophilic consolidation, often in several lobes and often bilateral and basal. Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are typical causes. Pseudomonas bronchopneumonia is classic in hospitalized, ventilated, or cystic fibrosis patients. Staphylococcus aureus can also form abscesses and thin-walled pneumatoceles, as in this patient.
whyNot: Coxiella burnetii, the cause of Q fever, is inhaled in dust from infected farm animals and their birth products. It causes atypical interstitial pneumonia, often with hepatitis, not patchy purulent bronchopneumonia.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia with an interstitial, mononuclear infiltrate in the alveolar septa and little alveolar exudate.
Chlamydophila (Chlamydia) pneumoniae also causes atypical interstitial pneumonia, usually a mild illness with patchy septal inflammation and no purulent alveolar exudate.
Correct.

questions.stem: She asks why a new influenza vaccine is needed every year even though the same influenza A subtype has circulated for several seasons. Which of the following properties of the virus best explains the need for annual reformulation?
options: Point mutations in surface glycoprotein genes
Reassortment of genome segments with avian strains
Phase variation in expression of surface proteins
Gene conversion among silent antigen gene copies
approach: Same subtype, gradual change each year: that describes antigenic drift.
Influenza is a segmented negative-sense RNA virus whose RNA-dependent RNA polymerase has no proofreading.
Point mutations accumulate in the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes and change the antibody-binding sites a little each season.
questions.why: Influenza A has eight segments of negative-sense RNA. Its RNA polymerase makes frequent copying errors, so point mutations accumulate in the genes for hemagglutinin (which binds sialic acid on airway cells) and neuraminidase (which releases new virions). Small changes in these surface proteins let the virus partly escape antibodies from earlier infection or vaccination. This antigenic drift causes yearly epidemics within the same subtype and is why the vaccine is updated every season.
whyNot: Correct.

Reassortment of whole segments between human and animal strains is antigenic shift. It creates a new subtype, can cause pandemics, and happens only occasionally, so it does not explain yearly change within one subtype.
Phase variation, switching a surface protein on or off, is a bacterial strategy, for example with Neisseria pili and opacity proteins.
Gene conversion from silent gene copies drives antigenic variation in organisms such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae pilin and Trypanosoma brucei. Influenza does not carry silent antigen genes.

questions.stem: As her blood passes through the pulmonary capillaries and hemoglobin binds oxygen, which of the following changes in the red cell most directly helps her eliminate carbon dioxide?
options: Increased carbamino binding of CO2 to globin chains
Increased binding of 2,3-BPG to deoxyhemoglobin
H+ release from hemoglobin, converting HCO3- to CO2
Movement of chloride from plasma into the red cell
approach: Oxygen binding in the lung is the setting for the Haldane effect.
Oxyhemoglobin holds H+ and CO2 less tightly than deoxyhemoglobin.
Released H+ combines with bicarbonate to form carbonic acid, and carbonic anhydrase turns it into CO2 and water. The CO2 diffuses into the alveoli.
questions.why: The Haldane effect states that oxygenation of hemoglobin lowers its affinity for CO2 and H+. In the lungs, hemoglobin releases H+ as it binds O2. The H+ combines with bicarbonate that has re-entered the red cell, and carbonic anhydrase converts the carbonic acid to CO2, which diffuses out to be exhaled. Carbamino CO2 is also released from oxyhemoglobin. The Bohr effect is the mirror image in the tissues: high CO2 and H+ lower hemoglobin's O2 affinity and help unload O2.
whyNot: Carbamino binding increases in the tissues, where hemoglobin is deoxygenated. In the lungs oxygenation lowers carbamino binding and CO2 is released.
2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and shifts the curve right. Its binding falls as hemoglobin is oxygenated, and it does not carry CO2.
Correct.
Chloride enters red cells in the systemic capillaries. In the lungs the chloride shift reverses: bicarbonate enters the red cell and chloride leaves.

case: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of sore throat, malaise, and painful neck swelling for 3 days. His parents declined all childhood vaccinations. His temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a gray-white membrane covering both tonsils and the posterior pharyngeal wall; it is firmly adherent and bleeds when scraped. There is marked cervical lymphadenopathy with diffuse soft tissue swelling of the anterior neck. Gram stain of material from beneath the membrane shows gram-positive club-shaped rods. Culture on tellurite agar grows gray-black colonies, and an Elek immunodiffusion test of the isolate is positive. The diagnosis is respiratory diphtheria.

questions.stem: Three weeks later, his throat has healed, but his speech is nasal and liquids come out of his nose when he swallows. The soft palate does not elevate during phonation. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Retropharyngeal abscess compressing the vagus nerve
Toxin-mediated demyelination of cranial nerves
Enteroviral destruction of brainstem motor neurons
approach: Palatal paralysis a few weeks after diphtheria is the classic first neurologic complication.
Diphtheria toxin travels in the blood and injures tissues away from the throat, mainly heart and nerves.
In nerves the toxin damages Schwann cells, causing demyelination that starts with the cranial nerves to the palate and pharynx.
questions.why: Diphtheria toxin is absorbed from the pharynx into the blood. Cells that take it up stop making protein and die. In peripheral nerves, injury to Schwann cells causes demyelinating neuropathy. Palatal paralysis is typically the first sign, in the second or third week, and may be followed by paralysis of eye movement or accommodation and later by a peripheral polyneuropathy. Myocarditis with conduction block is the other major toxin-mediated complication, usually about 1 to 2 weeks into the illness, and it is the main cause of death.
whyNot: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, which produces fatigable weakness, often with ptosis and diplopia. It is not a complication of diphtheria.
A retropharyngeal abscess causes fever, neck stiffness, and painful swallowing with a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall. His throat has healed, and the timing fits a toxin effect.
Correct.
Poliovirus, an enterovirus, can destroy brainstem motor neurons in bulbar polio. He has no history of a new febrile viral illness, and the setting points to diphtheria toxin.

questions.stem: A nontoxigenic strain of the same species is later isolated from a classmate's throat and causes only mild pharyngitis. The positive Elek test in this patient indicates production of a toxin that kills pharyngeal epithelial cells by which of the following mechanisms?
options: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2
ADP-ribosylation of the Gi alpha subunit
Cleavage of 28S ribosomal RNA
Proteolytic cleavage of SNARE proteins
approach: A strain that lacks the toxin causes only mild disease, so the toxin causes the membrane and the systemic damage.
The tox gene is carried by a lysogenic beta-prophage, so only lysogenized strains are toxigenic.
The toxin's A subunit ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, halting protein synthesis and killing the cell.
questions.why: Diphtheria toxin is an A-B exotoxin encoded by a gene carried on a beta-prophage. The B subunit binds a receptor on host cells and allows entry. The A subunit then ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, which stops translation. Local epithelial death plus fibrin, neutrophils, and bacteria forms the adherent pseudomembrane. Absorbed toxin damages heart and nerves. The Elek test detects toxin production by a precipitin line between the isolate and antitoxin.
whyNot: Correct.
ADP-ribosylation of Gi is the action of pertussis toxin. It raises cAMP and causes lymphocytosis, but it does not stop protein synthesis.
Removing an adenine from 28S ribosomal RNA of the 60S subunit is how Shiga toxin and Shiga-like toxin stop protein synthesis. Those toxins come from Shigella and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli.
Cleavage of SNARE proteins is the action of tetanus and botulinum toxins, which block neurotransmitter release rather than kill epithelial cells.

questions.stem: His 15-year-old cousin, who completed the recommended childhood immunization series, shares his bedroom. A throat culture from the cousin grows toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae, but she has no symptoms. Which of the following best explains her protection from disease?
options: Secretory IgA preventing colonization of the pharynx
Cytotoxic T cells killing infected epithelial cells
Opsonizing IgG against the bacterial capsule
Circulating IgG that neutralizes the toxin
approach: She is colonized but not sick, so her immunity blocks the toxin rather than the organism.
The diphtheria vaccine is a toxoid, a toxin inactivated with formaldehyde that keeps its antigenic structure.
Toxoid induces T-cell dependent IgG antitoxin that binds the toxin and prevents it from entering cells.
questions.why: Toxoid vaccines (diphtheria, tetanus) present inactivated toxin protein. Because it is a protein, helper T cells support class switching and memory, giving long-lived IgG antitoxin. Antitoxin binds circulating toxin and blocks its attachment and entry, so the toxin cannot cause the membrane, myocarditis, or neuropathy. Toxoid immunity does not reliably prevent colonization, which is why vaccinated people can carry toxigenic strains. This contrasts with polysaccharide vaccines, which are T-cell independent and give weak, short-lived IgM responses unless the polysaccharide is conjugated to a protein carrier.
whyNot: Toxoid vaccination does not target the organism, so it does little to prevent colonization. Her positive culture shows the bacteria are present in her pharynx.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae stays on the mucosal surface and does not invade cells, so cytotoxic T cells are not the defense. The vaccine is directed at the toxin.

Opsonizing anticapsular antibody is the goal of polysaccharide and conjugate vaccines such as those for pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b. The diphtheria vaccine contains no bacterial capsule.
Correct.

topics: T-cell dependent versus independent antibody responses

questions.stem: Indirect mirror examination shows that the membrane extends upward behind the soft palate onto the lateral walls of the nasopharynx. Spread of infection through openings in this region most directly places him at risk for which of the following?
options: Dacryocystitis
Otitis media
Maxillary sinusitis
Parotitis
approach: Locate the region: above the soft palate and behind the nasal cavity is the nasopharynx.
The pharyngotympanic (auditory) tube opens on each lateral wall of the nasopharynx, behind the torus tubarius.
The tube connects to the middle ear, so infection or obstruction here leads to otitis media.
questions.why: The pharynx has three parts: the nasopharynx above the soft palate, the oropharynx from the soft palate to the epiglottis, and the laryngopharynx below. The nasopharynx contains the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) on its posterior wall and the openings of the pharyngotympanic tubes on its lateral walls, with the tubal tonsils nearby. Swelling or infection here can block the tube or spread into the middle ear. This is also why enlarged adenoids in children cause otitis media, mouth breathing, and snoring. The palatine tonsils lie in the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
whyNot: The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity, not the nasopharynx. Dacryocystitis follows obstruction of that duct.
Correct.
The maxillary sinus drains into the middle meatus of the nasal cavity, so nasopharyngeal spread would not reach it directly.
The parotid duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar, far from the nasopharynx.

dx: Disseminated histoplasmosis in a man with AIDS
case: A 41-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago comes to the physician because of fever, cough, and 8-kg weight loss over 5 weeks. He lives in rural Kentucky and recently cleaned out an old chicken coop. His temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 106/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Examination shows a shallow ulcer on the tongue, generalized lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 32/mm3 (500 to 1,500). Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), leukocyte count is 2,900/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), and platelet count is 74,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). A chest x-ray shows diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates. Urine Histoplasma antigen is positive. The diagnosis is disseminated histoplasmosis.

questions.stem: Most people in his region who inhale this organism have no symptoms or a brief, self-limited illness. Which of the following best explains why the infection disseminated in this patient?
options: Absent interferon-gamma activation of macrophages
Absence of complement-mediated lysis of the yeast
Defective NADPH oxidase activity in neutrophils
Deficient secretory IgA at the bronchial mucosa
approach: Histoplasma yeasts live inside macrophages, so control depends on cell-mediated immunity.
In healthy hosts, CD4+ Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill the yeasts and form granulomas that wall off the infection.
With a CD4 count of 32/mm3, this does not happen, so infected macrophages carry the organism to the liver, spleen, marrow, and lymph nodes.
questions.why: Histoplasma capsulatum is inhaled as microconidia, which convert to yeasts inside alveolar macrophages. In healthy people, Th1 cells produce interferon-gamma that activates macrophages, and granulomas contain the infection. These granulomas can caseate and later calcify in the lung and hilar nodes, mimicking tuberculosis. When CD4+ T cells are severely depleted, macrophages cannot kill the yeasts and spread them through the reticuloendothelial system. This produces fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia from marrow involvement, and mucosal ulcers. Endemic fungi can also disseminate to skin, bone, and meninges.
whyNot: Correct.
Complement lysis is a key defense against Neisseria and other gram-negative bacteria. Fungal cell walls resist the membrane attack complex, and complement is not the defect in AIDS.
Defective NADPH oxidase is chronic granulomatous disease. It predisposes to catalase-positive organisms such as Aspergillus and Staphylococcus aureus, not to the loss of T-cell help seen here.
Secretory IgA deficiency causes recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections. It does not explain spread of an intracellular yeast through the macrophage system.

questions.stem: A bone marrow biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Large yeasts with broad-based budding
Thick-walled spherules filled with endospores
Small oval yeasts within macrophages
Narrow-based budding yeasts with a thick capsule
approach: Use the clues: Ohio and Mississippi River valley region, bird or bat droppings, and spread through the macrophage system point to Histoplasma.
Recall the tissue form of each dimorphic fungus.
Histoplasma appears as small (about 2 to 4 µm) oval yeasts packed inside macrophages.
questions.why: The dimorphic fungi grow as molds in the environment and as yeasts or spherules in tissue. Histoplasma capsulatum is found in soil enriched with bird or bat droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. In tissue it is a small intracellular yeast filling macrophages, which is why it spreads to marrow, liver, spleen, and nodes. Blastomyces (Great Lakes and Ohio and Mississippi basins) forms large broad-based budding yeasts, and Coccidioides (southwestern United States) forms spherules containing endospores.
whyNot: Large yeasts with broad-based budding are Blastomyces dermatitidis, which often spreads to skin and bone. It is extracellular and much larger than Histoplasma.
Spherules with endospores are Coccidioides immitis, found in the desert soil of the southwestern United States.
Correct.
Narrow-based budding yeasts with a thick polysaccharide capsule are Cryptococcus neoformans, which causes meningitis in AIDS and is found in pigeon droppings worldwide.

questions.stem: His physician also notes that he stopped taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis when he stopped antiretroviral therapy. The opportunistic fungal pneumonia this drug was meant to prevent typically presents with which of the following?
options: Mobile mass within an old upper lobe cavity
Bilateral ground-glass opacities, exertional hypoxemia
Nodules with surrounding halo during prolonged neutropenia
Fleeting infiltrates with eosinophilia in asthma
approach: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis is given when the CD4 count falls below 200/mm3 to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
Pneumocystis fills alveoli with a foamy exudate and causes diffuse interstitial and alveolar disease.
The result is bilateral ground-glass infiltrates, a dry cough, oxygen desaturation with exertion, and a high serum LDH.
questions.why: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia occurs mainly when the CD4 count is below 200/mm3. It begins gradually with dry cough, fever, and dyspnea. Chest imaging shows bilateral, often perihilar, ground-glass opacities, and oxygen saturation falls sharply with exertion. Serum LDH is usually high. Silver stain of lavage fluid shows the cysts. Aspergillus causes different patterns that depend on the host: a fungus ball in an old cavity, angioinvasive disease in neutropenia, and allergic disease in asthma or cystic fibrosis.
whyNot: A mobile fungus ball in a preexisting cavity is an aspergilloma. It needs no immune defect and often presents with hemoptysis.
Correct.
Nodules with a halo of hemorrhage during prolonged neutropenia suggest invasive aspergillosis. Neutrophils, not CD4+ T cells, are the main defense against Aspergillus hyphae.
Fleeting infiltrates with eosinophilia and high IgE in a patient with asthma or cystic fibrosis describe allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, a hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.stem: A CT scan shows enlarged lymph nodes at both lung hila. Compared with the right hilum, which of the following arrangements is characteristic of the normal left hilum?
options: Eparterial lobar bronchus above the pulmonary artery
Pulmonary veins superior to the main bronchus
Main bronchus anterior to the pulmonary veins
Pulmonary artery superior to the main bronchus
approach: At each hilum the pulmonary veins are the most anterior and inferior structures.
On the right, the superior lobar (eparterial) bronchus branches early and lies above the pulmonary artery, which runs anterior to the bronchus.
On the left there is no eparterial bronchus, so the pulmonary artery arches over the main bronchus and is the most superior structure.
questions.why: The root of each lung contains the pulmonary artery, the main bronchus, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, and lymphatics, with hilar lymph nodes around them. In both hila the pulmonary veins lie anterior and inferior. On the left, the pulmonary artery lies superior to the main bronchus. On the right, the superior lobar bronchus comes off above the pulmonary artery, so the right pulmonary artery lies anterior to the bronchus. Enlarged hilar nodes from granulomatous infections or lymphoma sit among these structures.
whyNot: An eparterial bronchus above the pulmonary artery describes the right hilum, where the superior lobar bronchus branches above the artery.
The pulmonary veins are the most inferior structures at both hila.
The pulmonary veins are anterior to the bronchus at both hila, so the bronchus is posterior to them.
Correct.

case: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 days after the sudden onset of a shaking chill, fever, and sharp right-sided chest pain on inspiration. She now has a cough productive of rust-colored sputum. Her temperature is 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Over the right lower posterior chest there is dullness to percussion, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, and egophony. Leukocyte count is 19,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) with 14% band forms. Arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.31 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 33 mm Hg (35 to 45), and PaO2 61 mm Hg (75 to 100). A chest x-ray shows consolidation of the entire right lower lobe with air bronchograms. Sputum Gram stain shows gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci, and a urine pneumococcal antigen test is positive. The diagnosis is lobar pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae.

questions.stem: Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative gram-positive cocci. Which of the following results for this isolate would best distinguish it from viridans streptococci?
options: Growth in 6.5% NaCl
Resistance to optochin
Hydrolysis of esculin
Solubility in bile
approach: Alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative cocci are either Streptococcus pneumoniae or viridans streptococci.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is optochin sensitive and bile soluble, and viridans streptococci are optochin resistant and bile insoluble.
Of the choices, only bile solubility points to pneumococcus.
questions.why: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococcus that is catalase negative and alpha-hemolytic. It is lysed by bile salts because they activate its own autolysin, and it is inhibited by optochin. Viridans streptococci share the alpha-hemolysis but resist both. The pneumococcal polysaccharide capsule is its main virulence factor because it blocks phagocytosis, and IgA protease helps it colonize the nasopharynx. It is the most common cause of community-acquired and lobar pneumonia.
whyNot: Growth in 6.5% NaCl identifies Enterococcus, which is usually gamma-hemolytic and causes urinary tract infections and endocarditis, not lobar pneumonia.
Optochin resistance is the result viridans streptococci give. This isolate is pneumococcus, which is optochin sensitive.
Esculin hydrolysis in bile is used to identify group D streptococci and enterococci, not to separate pneumococcus from viridans streptococci.
Correct.

questions.stem: If the consolidated lobe were examined at this point in her illness, which of the following findings would most likely be seen?
options: Vascular engorgement with serous fluid and few neutrophils
Alveoli filled with neutrophils, erythrocytes, and fibrin
Disintegrating erythrocytes in a fibrinosuppurative exudate
Enzymatic digestion of exudate with restored architecture
approach: Her illness began 3 days ago, so place her on the timeline of untreated lobar pneumonia.
Congestion lasts about the first 1 to 2 days, red hepatization about days 2 to 4, gray hepatization about days 4 to 8, then resolution.
At day 3 the lobe is in red hepatization: airless, red, firm, and liver-like, with alveoli packed with neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin.
questions.why: Lobar pneumonia passes through four classic stages. In congestion the lobe is heavy and wet, with engorged capillaries, edema fluid, many bacteria, and few neutrophils. In red hepatization the alveoli fill with neutrophils, extravasated red cells, and fibrin, so the lobe looks red and firm like liver. The red cells explain the rust-colored sputum. In gray hepatization the red cells break down and a fibrinosuppurative exudate remains. In resolution enzymes digest the exudate and the architecture is restored. A uniformly consolidated lobe produces dullness, increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, and egophony.
whyNot: Engorgement with serous fluid and few neutrophils is the congestion stage of about the first 1 to 2 days. It would not yet give the firm consolidation and rusty sputum she has.
Correct.
Breakdown of red cells in a fibrinosuppurative exudate is gray hepatization, at about days 4 to 8.
Enzymatic digestion with restored architecture is resolution, which follows the hepatization stages.

questions.stem: Her fever and acidemia alter how hemoglobin releases oxygen in her tissues. Which of the following best describes this change?
options: Stabilization of the relaxed (R) state, lowering P50
Loss of cooperative binding, producing a hyperbolic curve
Stabilization of the taut (T) state, raising P50
Lower oxygen-binding capacity with unchanged P50
approach: Fever and a low pH (high H+) both shift the oxyhemoglobin curve to the right.
A right shift means lower O2 affinity, so a higher PO2 is needed for 50% saturation (higher P50).
Lower affinity reflects stabilization of the deoxygenated taut (T) state, which favors O2 unloading in the tissues.
questions.why: Hemoglobin has two conformations. The taut (T) state has low O2 affinity, and the relaxed (R) state has high affinity. Binding of one O2 favors the shift to R, which makes the next O2 bind more easily. This cooperative binding gives the sigmoid curve. Increased H+, CO2, temperature, and 2,3-BPG stabilize the T state, shift the curve right, and raise the P50 (normally about 27 mm Hg). This helps deliver O2 to hot, acidic, metabolically active tissues. Fetal hemoglobin, carbon monoxide, and methemoglobin shift the curve left.
whyNot: Stabilizing the R state and lowering P50 is a left shift. It is caused by low temperature, alkalosis, low 2,3-BPG, fetal hemoglobin, or carbon monoxide, which is the opposite of her state.
A hyperbolic curve without cooperativity is typical of myoglobin, which has one heme. Fever and acidemia shift hemoglobin's curve but keep its sigmoid shape.
Correct.
Lower binding capacity with an unchanged P50 is the pattern of anemia, where there is less hemoglobin but each molecule behaves normally.

topics: T and R states of hemoglobin

questions.stem: In her systemic capillaries, carbon dioxide from her metabolically active tissues diffuses into red blood cells. Which of the following events then occurs in these cells?
options: Chloride influx in exchange for bicarbonate
Bicarbonate influx in exchange for chloride
CO2 binding to the ferrous iron of heme
Water efflux causing red cell shrinkage
approach: Most CO2, about 70 percent, travels as bicarbonate, formed inside red cells by carbonic anhydrase.
CO2 plus water becomes carbonic acid, which splits into H+ (buffered by hemoglobin) and bicarbonate.
Bicarbonate leaves the cell through the band 3 anion exchanger, and chloride enters in exchange. This is the chloride shift.
questions.why: CO2 is carried in blood in three forms: bicarbonate (about 70 percent), carbaminohemoglobin bound to amino groups of globin (about 20 percent), and dissolved CO2 (about 10 percent). Red cell carbonic anhydrase rapidly converts CO2 and water to carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and bicarbonate. Deoxyhemoglobin buffers the H+. Bicarbonate moves to the plasma in exchange for chloride through band 3, so venous red cells contain more chloride. In the lungs every step runs in reverse.
whyNot: Correct.
Bicarbonate enters red cells in exchange for chloride in the pulmonary capillaries, where CO2 is being released. This is the reverse chloride shift.
CO2 binds the terminal amino groups of the globin chains to form carbaminohemoglobin. It does not bind heme iron, which is where O2 and carbon monoxide bind.
The added chloride and bicarbonate raise osmotic content, so water enters and venous red cells swell slightly. They do not shrink.

dx: Lung abscess after aspiration in a man with alcohol use disorder
case: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder comes to the physician because of 3 weeks of fever, night sweats, 5-kg weight loss, and cough productive of large amounts of foul-smelling, foul-tasting sputum. He reports several episodes of heavy drinking that ended with him waking on the floor. His temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. He has severe gingivitis and multiple carious teeth. Leukocyte count is 15,600/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). A chest x-ray shows a 5-cm thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level in the right lung. Sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils and mixed bacterial flora. The diagnosis is lung abscess after aspiration.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely source of the organisms that caused this abscess?
options: Hematogenous seeding from right-sided endocarditis
Anaerobic bacteria from the gingival crevices
Inhaled droplet nuclei from an infected contact
Aerosolized water from a contaminated cooling tower
approach: Episodes of lost consciousness from alcohol plus poor dentition set up aspiration of mouth contents.
Putrid sputum with mixed flora points to anaerobes, which make foul-smelling fatty acids and other metabolic products.
The gingival crevices of a mouth with periodontal disease hold large numbers of anaerobes such as Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Prevotella, and Peptostreptococcus.
questions.why: Most lung abscesses follow aspiration of oropharyngeal contents when consciousness or swallowing is impaired, as with alcohol intoxication, seizures, anesthesia, or dysphagia. Poor dental hygiene raises the anaerobic load. The anaerobes and mixed flora cause necrotizing pneumonia that liquefies into a cavity, which shows an air-fluid level once it drains into a bronchus. Foul sputum is the clinical clue. Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae can also cause abscesses, usually after a necrotizing pneumonia.
whyNot: Right-sided endocarditis, as in injection drug use, seeds the lungs with septic emboli. These appear as multiple peripheral nodules, often cavitating, and are usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
Correct.
Droplet nuclei from an infected contact transmit Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which forms apical cavities with chronic symptoms but does not produce putrid sputum or mixed flora.
Contaminated cooling towers and water systems transmit Legionella pneumophila, which causes pneumonia with hyponatremia and diarrhea, not a putrid anaerobic abscess.

questions.stem: He says he usually wakes from these episodes lying on his back. In which of the following bronchopulmonary segments is his abscess most likely located?
options: Superior segment of the right lower lobe
Anterior segment of the right upper lobe
Medial segment of the right middle lobe
Lateral basal segment of the left lower lobe
approach: Aspirated material favors the right side because the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left.
Material then follows gravity to the most dependent segment for the body position.
Lying supine, the posteriorly directed superior segmental bronchus of the right lower lobe is dependent, so material collects there.
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures, and the left lung has two lobes with the lingula and cardiac notch. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical, so aspirated material usually enters the right lung. Gravity then decides the segment. When upright, material reaches the basal segments of the right lower lobe. When supine, it enters the superior segment of the right lower lobe, and the posterior segment of the right upper lobe is the other classic supine site. When lying on the right side, the right upper lobe is favored.
whyNot: Correct.
The anterior segment of the right upper lobe points forward and upward, so it is not dependent when lying on the back.
The right middle lobe medial segment points forward. It is not dependent in the supine position and is an uncommon site for aspiration.
Aspiration favors the right lung, and the left lower lobe basal segments are dependent mainly in the upright position.

questions.stem: Ten days into treatment, he has new right-sided pleuritic pain and persistent fever. Ultrasound shows a loculated pleural collection. Thoracentesis yields thick yellow fluid with pH 6.9 (about 7.6 normally), glucose 22 mg/dL (serum 104 mg/dL), and LDH 2,400 U/L (serum upper limit 220 U/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chylothorax
Hemothorax
Hepatic hydrothorax
Empyema
approach: A pleural collection appearing during a lung infection raises concern for spread into the pleural space.
Very low pH and glucose with very high LDH mean intense neutrophil and bacterial metabolism in the fluid.
Thick, purulent, loculated fluid after pneumonia or abscess is empyema.
questions.why: Empyema is pus in the pleural space. It usually follows pneumonia or a lung abscess that ruptures or spreads to the pleura. Neutrophils and bacteria consume glucose and generate acid, so the fluid has low pH and glucose and very high LDH. Fibrin deposition causes loculation. Without drainage, organization can lead to a thick pleural peel that restricts lung expansion.
whyNot: Chylothorax is milky fluid with a high triglyceride level from thoracic duct injury or obstruction, as with trauma or lymphoma. It is not acidic or purulent.
Hemothorax is blood in the pleural space, usually after trauma, with a pleural fluid hematocrit at least half that of blood.
Hepatic hydrothorax is a transudate in cirrhosis from ascitic fluid crossing the diaphragm. It has normal pH and glucose and low LDH.
Correct.

questions.stem: The abscess heals, leaving a thin-walled residual cavity. Two years later he has recurrent small-volume hemoptysis. CT shows a round mass inside the cavity that moves when he changes position. Microscopy of the mass would most likely show which of the following?
options: Broad nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branches
Budding yeasts with pseudohyphae
Septate hyphae with acute-angle branches
Cysts on methenamine silver stain
approach: A mobile ball in an old cavity with hemoptysis is a fungus ball (aspergilloma).
Aspergillus colonizes the cavity without invading tissue, so it needs no immune defect.
Aspergillus forms septate hyphae that branch at acute angles, about 45 degrees.
questions.why: An aspergilloma is a tangled mass of Aspergillus hyphae growing in a preexisting cavity from tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, or a healed abscess. It moves with position and can erode vessels in the cavity wall, causing hemoptysis. Microscopy shows narrow, septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. The host defect decides other Aspergillus forms: neutropenia allows angioinvasive disease, while CD4 counts below 200/mm3 allow Pneumocystis, whose cysts stain with methenamine silver.
whyNot: Broad, ribbon-like, nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching are Mucor and Rhizopus, which invade tissue in diabetic ketoacidosis and neutropenia.
Budding yeasts with pseudohyphae are Candida, which rarely forms a pulmonary fungus ball and is usually found in the mouth, esophagus, or blood of compromised hosts.
Correct.
Cysts on methenamine silver stain are Pneumocystis jirovecii, which causes diffuse pneumonia with CD4 counts below 200/mm3, not a ball in a cavity.

case: A 7-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of spells of coughing followed by cyanosis and pauses in breathing. She had 10 days of runny nose and mild cough, and for the past 4 days she has had bursts of rapid coughs, often followed by vomiting. She was born at term and has not yet received any vaccines. Her mother has had a cough for 3 weeks and did not receive a pertussis vaccine during pregnancy. The infant's temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 160/min, and respirations are 48/min. Between spells she appears well, and the lungs are clear. Leukocyte count is 42,000/mm3 (5,000 to 19,500) with 76% lymphocytes. Nasopharyngeal PCR is positive for Bordetella pertussis. The diagnosis is pertussis.

questions.stem: Her mother's illness began with a week of rhinorrhea and mild cough, followed by 2 weeks of severe coughing fits. The mother was most likely to transmit the infection during which stage of her illness?
options: Incubation
Paroxysmal
Catarrhal
Convalescent
approach: Recall the three clinical stages: catarrhal (cold-like, 1 to 2 weeks), paroxysmal (coughing fits, whoop, posttussive vomiting, 2 to 6 weeks), and convalescent (slow fading of cough over weeks).
Bacterial numbers in the airway are highest early, in the catarrhal stage.
Because the symptoms then look like a common cold, the disease is rarely recognized while it is most contagious.
questions.why: Bordetella pertussis attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium and multiplies there. The catarrhal stage, with rhinorrhea, mild cough, and low-grade fever, carries the highest bacterial load and the greatest risk of spread. In the paroxysmal stage, toxin-mediated damage produces fits of rapid coughs followed by an inspiratory whoop and posttussive vomiting, while bacterial numbers fall. The convalescent stage brings slow recovery. Young infants often have no whoop and instead present with apnea, cyanosis, and a high risk of pneumonia and death.
whyNot: During incubation, about 7 to 10 days, the organism is establishing itself and there is little or no cough to spread it.
The paroxysmal stage is still contagious, but bacterial numbers are falling, and transmission is greatest earlier.
Correct.
In the convalescent stage the cough slowly fades, and the organism is usually no longer recoverable, so transmission is unlikely.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her leukocyte count?
options: Superantigen-driven polyclonal T-cell proliferation
Adenylate cyclase toxin stimulating marrow lymphopoiesis
Viral transformation of circulating B lymphocytes
ADP-ribosylation of Gi blocking lymphocyte homing
approach: Marked lymphocytosis is a classic finding in pertussis, especially in infants.
Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates the alpha subunit of Gi, so Gi can no longer inhibit adenylate cyclase.
Chemokine receptors on lymphocytes signal through Gi. Blocking this signal keeps lymphocytes from leaving the blood for lymph nodes and tissues, so they accumulate in circulation.
questions.why: Pertussis toxin is an A-B toxin. Its A subunit ADP-ribosylates Gi alpha, which locks it in the inactive state, so adenylate cyclase is no longer inhibited and cAMP rises. Lymphocytes depend on Gi-coupled chemokine receptors to home out of the blood, so they stay in circulation and produce marked lymphocytosis. The toxin also contributes to airway damage, insulin release with hypoglycemia, and impaired phagocyte function. In contrast, diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 and kills cells by stopping protein synthesis.
whyNot: Superantigens, such as toxic shock syndrome toxin, cross-link MHC class II and T-cell receptors outside the antigen groove. They cause cytokine storm and shock, not a sustained lymphocytosis.
Bordetella adenylate cyclase toxin enters phagocytes and raises their cAMP, which impairs killing. It does not stimulate the marrow to make lymphocytes.
Viral transformation of B cells is the action of Epstein-Barr virus, which causes infectious mononucleosis with atypical lymphocytes (mostly reactive T cells).
Correct.

questions.stem: If her mother had received the Tdap vaccine in the third trimester, which of the following would most likely have protected this infant during her first 2 months of life?
options: Transplacental IgG against pertussis toxin and adhesins
Maternal memory T cells crossing the placenta
Live attenuated bacteria colonizing the infant's nasopharynx
Infant IgM produced against vaccine polysaccharide
approach: The infant is too young to have been vaccinated, so any protection must come from the mother.
Tdap contains protein antigens: pertussis toxoid, filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and sometimes fimbriae. These give a T-cell dependent IgG response.
IgG is the only antibody class actively carried across the placenta, by the neonatal Fc receptor, mostly in the third trimester.
questions.why: Acellular pertussis vaccines contain purified protein antigens, including inactivated pertussis toxin and adhesins such as filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin. Because they are proteins, they drive T-cell dependent class switching to IgG with memory. When given at about 27 to 36 weeks of pregnancy, the mother's boosted IgG crosses the placenta through the neonatal Fc receptor. This passive antibody neutralizes toxin and blocks attachment, protecting the infant until her own DTaP series begins at 2 months. Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy for this reason.
whyNot: Correct.
Maternal T cells do not cross the placenta in useful numbers. Passive protection of the newborn is provided by antibody.
The acellular pertussis vaccine is not live. It contains purified, inactivated proteins and cannot colonize anyone.
Pertussis vaccines are protein vaccines, not polysaccharide vaccines. Polysaccharides give T-cell independent IgM responses, and infants under 2 years respond poorly to them.

questions.stem: During a coughing paroxysm her oxygen saturation falls to 74%. When the paroxysm ends, she takes several rapid, deep breaths. Which of the following receptors most directly sense the fall in arterial PO2 that drives this response?
options: Central chemoreceptors in the ventral medulla
Glomus cells of the carotid bodies
Pulmonary stretch receptors in airway smooth muscle
Juxtacapillary receptors in the alveolar walls
approach: A saturation of 74% means a PaO2 well below 60 mm Hg, which is the range where hypoxic drive becomes strong.
Only the peripheral chemoreceptors, the carotid and aortic bodies, respond to low arterial PO2.
Carotid body glomus cells depolarize when PO2 falls, and the glossopharyngeal nerve carries the signal to the medulla to increase ventilation.
questions.why: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic bodies (vagus nerve) respond mainly to a fall in arterial PO2 below about 60 mm Hg, where the oxyhemoglobin curve becomes steep. They also respond to rising PaCO2 and H+. Central chemoreceptors in the ventral medulla respond to H+ in the cerebrospinal fluid, formed when CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier. They control most of the minute-to-minute ventilation but do not sense oxygen. Hypoxemia and hypercapnia together raise ventilation more than either does alone.
whyNot: Central chemoreceptors respond to CSF H+ produced from arterial CO2. They are not stimulated by low PO2, and severe hypoxia actually depresses the medullary centers.
Correct.
Pulmonary stretch receptors sense lung inflation and terminate inspiration (the Hering-Breuer reflex). They do not measure blood gases.
Juxtacapillary (J) receptors sense interstitial fluid and congestion, as in pulmonary edema, and cause rapid shallow breathing. They do not detect arterial PO2.

dx: Respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis in a former preterm infant
case: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department in January because of cough, fast breathing, and poor feeding for 2 days after 3 days of nasal congestion. He was born at 30 weeks' gestation and now weighs 5 kg. His temperature is 38.0 °C (100.4 °F), pulse is 172/min, and respirations are 70/min. Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. He has nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal retractions, and diffuse expiratory wheezes and fine crackles. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflation with patchy peribronchial thickening. Nasopharyngeal PCR is positive for respiratory syncytial virus. The diagnosis is respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this virus causes severe airway obstruction in infants like him, while it usually causes only a cold in adults?
options: Surfactant deficiency causing diffuse alveolar collapse
Smooth muscle hypertrophy from chronic allergic inflammation
Loss of alveolar walls reducing elastic recoil
Edema and debris narrowing very small bronchioles
approach: Bronchiolitis means infection of the small airways, with epithelial necrosis, mucus, edema, and lymphocytic inflammation in the bronchioles.
Airway resistance rises steeply as radius falls (resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power).
Infant bronchioles are tiny, and a preterm infant's are smaller still, so the same amount of swelling and debris causes far more obstruction.
questions.why: Respiratory syncytial virus is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, with yearly winter epidemics. It infects bronchiolar epithelium, causing necrosis, sloughing, mucus plugs, submucosal edema, and peribronchiolar lymphocytes. In small airways these changes cause partial obstruction with air trapping and wheezing, or complete obstruction with atelectasis. Prematurity, chronic lung disease of prematurity, congenital heart disease, and age under about 6 months increase the risk of severe disease. Preterm infants also received less maternal IgG, which mostly crosses the placenta late in pregnancy.
whyNot: Surfactant deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in the first hours after preterm birth. At 4 months his surfactant system is mature, and his findings are airway obstruction rather than diffuse collapse.
Smooth muscle hypertrophy from chronic allergic inflammation is a feature of long-standing asthma. It develops over years and does not explain an acute viral illness in a 4-month-old.
Loss of alveolar walls with reduced elastic recoil is emphysema, a chronic disease of adults.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before the season, he could have received a preventive monoclonal antibody against this virus. This antibody neutralizes the virus by binding which of the following?
options: Hemagglutinin that binds sialic acid on airway cells
F protein that fuses viral and cell membranes
Neuraminidase that releases newly formed virions
Spike protein that binds ACE2 on host cells
approach: Respiratory syncytial virus is an enveloped, negative-sense RNA pneumovirus with two main surface glycoproteins, G (attachment) and F (fusion).
The F protein fuses the viral envelope with the host cell membrane and also fuses neighboring infected cells into syncytia, which gives the virus its name.
Preventive monoclonal antibodies such as palivizumab and nirsevimab bind the F protein and block entry and cell-to-cell spread.
questions.why: Respiratory syncytial virus is a nonsegmented negative-sense RNA virus, now classed as a pneumovirus and formerly as a paramyxovirus. Its F protein drives fusion of viral and cell membranes and forms multinucleated syncytia. It has no hemagglutinin or neuraminidase. F is well conserved, which makes it the target of preventive monoclonal antibodies and of maternal and older-adult vaccines. Influenza, by contrast, uses hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, and SARS-CoV-2 uses its spike protein to bind ACE2.
whyNot: Hemagglutinin binding sialic acid is how influenza attaches to cells. Respiratory syncytial virus lacks a hemagglutinin.
Correct.
Neuraminidase, which cleaves sialic acid to release new virions, is an influenza protein and the target of oseltamivir. Respiratory syncytial virus does not have it.
Spike protein binding ACE2 is the entry mechanism of SARS-CoV-2, an enveloped positive-sense RNA coronavirus.

questions.stem: Before this illness, at rest he breathed 40 times per minute with a tidal volume of 35 mL. He now breathes 70 times per minute with a tidal volume of 18 mL. Assume his dead space remains 10 mL. Which of the following is his current alveolar ventilation, in mL/min?
approach: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume minus dead space) x respiratory rate.
Now: (18 mL minus 10 mL) x 70/min = 560 mL/min.

Compare with before: (35 minus 10) x 40 = 1,000 mL/min. His minute ventilation fell only slightly, from 1,400 to 1,260 mL/min, but alveolar ventilation fell by almost half because more of each small breath is dead space.
questions.why: Minute ventilation is tidal volume times rate. Alveolar ventilation subtracts the dead space from each breath, because dead space air never reaches gas exchange. With rapid shallow breathing, the fixed dead space takes up a larger share of each breath. Here the dead-space fraction rose from about 29% to about 56%, so alveolar ventilation fell from 1,000 to 560 mL/min. That fall raises PaCO2. Physiologic dead space can be measured with the Bohr equation: VD/VT = (PaCO2 minus PECO2) / PaCO2.
whyNot: Correct.
700 mL/min is the dead space ventilation (10 mL x 70/min), the part of each minute's breathing that does not reach alveoli.
1,000 mL/min was his alveolar ventilation before the illness, at 40 breaths per minute with a 35-mL tidal volume.
1,260 mL/min is his current minute ventilation (18 mL x 70/min). It ignores the dead space.

topics: Rapid shallow breathing and dead space

questions.stem: At age 8 years, he has recurrent wheezing, and air trapping is suspected. Which of the following lung volumes must be measured by helium dilution or body plethysmography rather than by spirometry?
options: Vital capacity
Inspiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Expiratory reserve volume
approach: Air trapping means gas stays in the lungs after a full exhalation, so the key volume is residual volume.
A spirometer measures only air that moves in or out of the mouth.
Residual volume never leaves the lungs, so it needs gas dilution or plethysmography, and so do FRC and TLC, which contain it.
questions.why: Tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and vital capacity can all be measured with spirometry because they are exhaled. Residual volume is the air left after maximal exhalation. Functional residual capacity (expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume) and total lung capacity also include it. Helium dilution measures the gas volume that the helium mixes into, and body plethysmography uses Boyle's law to measure all thoracic gas. In obstructive disease with air trapping, residual volume and the ratio of residual volume to total lung capacity rise.
whyNot: Vital capacity is the largest volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration, so spirometry measures it directly.
Inspiratory reserve volume is extra air inhaled above a normal tidal breath, and a spirometer records it.
Correct.
Expiratory reserve volume is the extra air exhaled after a normal tidal exhalation. It leaves the lungs, so spirometry measures it.

case: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis comes to the physician because of cough, low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, and 6-kg weight loss over 2 months. For the past week her sputum has been streaked with blood. Five months ago she began treatment with a tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitor. She received BCG vaccine as an infant. Her temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over the right upper chest. A chest x-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the apical-posterior right upper lobe. Sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli, and a nucleic acid amplification test is positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. The diagnosis is reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis.

questions.stem: Three weeks after starting treatment, she develops progressive midback pain. There is tenderness over the T10 spinous process. MRI shows destruction of the T9 and T10 vertebral bodies and the intervening disc, with a paraspinal fluid collection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osteoporotic compression fracture
Metastatic adenocarcinoma
Multiple myeloma
Tuberculous spondylitis
approach: Active tuberculosis plus immunosuppression raises the risk of hematogenous spread beyond the lung.
Destruction of two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them, with a paraspinal (cold) abscess, is the classic pattern of spinal infection.
In this setting the diagnosis is tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease), most common in the lower thoracic spine.
questions.why: Reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis usually arises in the lung apices, where it forms caseating, cavitating lesions with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis. Bacilli can spread through the blood to the kidneys, meninges, adrenals, and vertebrae, especially when immunity is weakened by HIV, glucocorticoids, or TNF-alpha inhibitors. TNF-alpha helps keep granulomas intact, so blocking it allows latent foci to reactivate. In the spine, infection destroys vertebral bodies and the disc and may form a paraspinal or psoas cold abscess. Collapse can cause kyphosis and spinal cord compression.
whyNot: Osteoporotic fractures collapse a vertebral body but spare the disc and do not form a paraspinal fluid collection.
Metastatic carcinoma destroys vertebral bodies and pedicles but characteristically spares the intervertebral disc.
Multiple myeloma causes punched-out lytic lesions and fractures without disc destruction or abscess, usually with anemia, renal injury, and a monoclonal protein.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before she began the TNF-alpha inhibitor, she should have been screened for latent tuberculosis infection. Given her vaccination history, which of the following tests would have been the most specific for latent infection?
options: Tuberculin skin test
Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear
Interferon-gamma release assay
Serum antimycobacterial IgG titer
approach: Latent tuberculosis means contained infection with memory T cells, no symptoms, and no bacilli in sputum.
The tuberculin skin test uses purified protein derivative, which shares antigens with BCG, so it can be positive from vaccination.
The interferon-gamma release assay measures T-cell interferon-gamma release to ESAT-6 and CFP-10, antigens absent from BCG, so it is not confounded by vaccination.
questions.why: In primary tuberculosis, inhaled bacilli form a Ghon focus, usually in the lower part of an upper lobe or the upper part of a lower lobe, and spread to hilar nodes. Together these form the Ghon complex. Th1 cells then activate macrophages, and caseating granulomas contain the infection, which often calcifies (Ranke complex) and stays latent. Both screening tests detect this T-cell memory. The skin test is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction read as induration at 48 to 72 hours, and it can be falsely positive after BCG. The interferon-gamma release assay uses antigens found in M. tuberculosis but not in BCG, so it is more specific in vaccinated people. Neither test separates latent from active disease.
whyNot: The tuberculin skin test detects the same T-cell memory, but BCG shares its antigens and can cause a false-positive result in vaccinated people.
Sputum smears detect active pulmonary disease with many bacilli. In latent infection there are no bacilli in the sputum, so the smear is negative.
Correct.
Antibody tests are unreliable for tuberculosis because protection and memory are cell mediated. Serologic tests are not recommended for diagnosis or screening.

topics: Primary tuberculosis and the Ghon complex

questions.stem: After inhalation, the organism survives and multiplies inside alveolar macrophages. Which of the following mechanisms most directly allows this?
options: Escape from the phagosome into the cytosol
Inhibition of phagosome-lysosome fusion
Polysaccharide capsule that prevents ingestion
Protein A binding the Fc portion of IgG
approach: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is readily ingested by alveolar macrophages, so the question is how it avoids being killed afterward.
It stays inside the phagosome but prevents it from fusing with lysosomes and becoming acidic.
The bacteria then multiply within the protected phagosome until Th1 cells arrive and activate the macrophage.
questions.why: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is spread by airborne droplet nuclei small enough to reach the alveoli. Its waxy cell wall, rich in mycolic acids, makes it acid-fast and resistant to drying and to many disinfectants. Sulfatides and other wall components prevent phagosome-lysosome fusion, so it survives inside unactivated macrophages. Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) causes the serpentine growth pattern in culture, injures macrophages, and helps induce granuloma formation. Infection is controlled only after interferon-gamma from Th1 cells activates macrophages.
whyNot: Escape from the phagosome into the cytosol is used by Listeria monocytogenes (with listeriolysin O) and Shigella. Mycobacteria stay inside the phagosome.
Correct.
A polysaccharide capsule that blocks ingestion is the strategy of Streptococcus pneumoniae and Klebsiella. Mycobacteria are readily ingested and survive inside the cell.
Protein A binding the Fc portion of IgG is a Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor that blocks opsonization.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why reactivation tuberculosis favors the apices of the lungs in an upright person?
options: Highest ventilation-perfusion ratio and alveolar PO2
Greatest blood flow delivering more bacilli per minute
Lowest ventilation-perfusion ratio with alveolar hypoxia
Greatest ventilation per alveolus during tidal breathing
approach: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe, so it grows best where alveolar PO2 is highest.
When upright, gravity lowers arterial pressure at the apex, so perfusion falls much more than ventilation. The apex is usually in zone 2.
Apical V/Q is therefore the highest in the lung, about 3, and alveolar PO2 is highest, about 130 mm Hg.
questions.why: West zones describe how perfusion varies with height in the upright lung. In zone 1 (only in abnormal states, such as low arterial pressure or high alveolar pressure), alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure and there is no flow. In zone 2, arterial pressure exceeds alveolar pressure, which exceeds venous pressure, so flow depends on the arterial minus alveolar difference. In zone 3 at the base, arterial and venous pressures both exceed alveolar pressure and flow is greatest. Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the base, but perfusion changes more, so V/Q is highest at the apex and lowest at the base. The high apical PO2 suits the aerobic tubercle bacillus.
whyNot: Correct.
Blood flow is lowest at the apex in an upright person, not highest. Zone 3 at the base receives the most flow.
The lowest V/Q and lowest alveolar PO2 are found at the base, which is not where reactivation tuberculosis develops.
Ventilation per alveolus is greater at the base, because basal alveoli start smaller and sit on a steeper part of the pressure-volume curve.

dx: COVID-19 pneumonia progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome
case: A 69-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity is brought to the emergency department because of worsening shortness of breath. Eight days ago he developed fever, dry cough, fatigue, and loss of smell. His temperature is 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Crackles are heard over both lungs. He is intubated, and arterial PaO2 is 72 mm Hg on an FiO2 of 0.6. D-dimer is 3.8 µg/mL (below 0.5). A chest x-ray shows bilateral, mainly peripheral opacities. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function. Nasopharyngeal PCR is positive for SARS-CoV-2. The diagnosis is COVID-19 pneumonia complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: This virus infects alveolar type II pneumocytes and cells of the olfactory epithelium. Which of the following host molecules does it bind to enter these cells?
options: Sialic acid residues on glycoproteins
Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2
Intercellular adhesion molecule 1
CD4 glycoprotein
approach: SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped positive-sense RNA coronavirus whose spike protein mediates entry.
The spike receptor-binding domain attaches to ACE2, and host proteases such as TMPRSS2 then prime the spike for membrane fusion.
ACE2 is expressed on type II pneumocytes, nasal epithelium, and supporting cells of the olfactory epithelium, which explains pneumonia and loss of smell.
questions.why: Coronaviruses are enveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses. Common cold strains cause mild upper respiratory infections. SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 cause severe pneumonia. SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2 through its spike protein. Infection of olfactory supporting cells causes loss of smell, and infection of type II pneumocytes leads to diffuse alveolar damage. Endothelial injury and inflammation promote clotting, so D-dimer rises and venous and arterial thrombosis are common. Older age, diabetes, obesity, and heart and lung disease are major risk factors for severe disease.
whyNot: Sialic acid residues are the receptor for influenza hemagglutinin.
Correct.
ICAM-1 is the receptor for most rhinoviruses, a common cause of colds.
CD4, with CCR5 or CXCR4 as coreceptor, is the receptor for HIV on helper T cells and macrophages.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of his pulmonary edema?
options: Elevated pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
Obstruction of pulmonary lymphatic drainage
Increased alveolar-capillary permeability
approach: His PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 72/0.6 = 120, well below 300, with bilateral opacities within a week of a known insult.
Normal left ventricular function argues against cardiogenic (hydrostatic) edema.
This is acute respiratory distress syndrome: injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane lets protein-rich fluid leak into the alveoli.
questions.why: Acute respiratory distress syndrome follows a direct lung insult such as pneumonia or aspiration, or an indirect one such as sepsis, trauma, or pancreatitis. Injury to endothelium and type I pneumocytes, amplified by neutrophils and their proteases and oxygen radicals, makes the alveolar-capillary barrier leaky. Protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli, and fibrin and necrotic cell debris form hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage). The result is bilateral infiltrates and severe hypoxemia from shunt, with PaO2/FiO2 of 300 or less, not explained by heart failure. Survivors may develop interstitial fibrosis.
whyNot: High capillary hydrostatic pressure from left heart failure causes cardiogenic edema. His left ventricular function is normal.
Low plasma oncotic pressure, as in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis, causes transudative edema. It would not produce acute, severe hypoxemia after a viral pneumonia.
Lymphatic obstruction, as in lymphangitic carcinomatosis, causes slowly progressive interstitial thickening, not acute flooding of the alveoli.
Correct.

questions.stem: Fluid and hyaline membranes have thickened the barrier that oxygen must cross to reach his blood. In the normal lung, which of the following layers make up the thinnest part of this barrier?
options: Type II pneumocyte, interstitial fibroblast, endothelium
Type I pneumocyte, smooth muscle, endothelium
Type I pneumocyte, fused basement membranes, endothelium
Ciliated epithelium, lamina propria, endothelium
approach: Gas exchange happens across the thin portion of the alveolar wall.
Type I pneumocytes are flat cells covering about 95 percent of the alveolar surface, and type II cells are cuboidal and make surfactant.
At the thin part, the type I cell and capillary endothelium share one fused basement membrane, a barrier only about 0.2 to 0.6 µm thick.
questions.why: The blood-air barrier at its thinnest consists of the type I pneumocyte cytoplasm, the fused basement membranes of epithelium and endothelium, and the capillary endothelial cell, with a thin surfactant layer on the alveolar side. By Fick's law, diffusion is inversely proportional to barrier thickness. Edema, hyaline membranes, inflammatory cells, or interstitial fibrosis thicken it and slow diffusion of O2 more than CO2, because CO2 is far more soluble. The thicker part of the wall holds interstitial cells and fibers but is not the main site of gas exchange.
whyNot: Type II pneumocytes and fibroblasts are found in the thicker part of the wall. Type II cells make surfactant and repair the epithelium, but gas exchange happens across type I cells.
Alveolar walls contain no smooth muscle layer. Smooth muscle ends at the level of the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar duct openings.
Correct.
Ciliated epithelium and lamina propria line the conducting airways, which do not exchange gas.

questions.stem: On the ventilator, a higher pressure than normal is needed to deliver each tidal volume, and many alveoli collapse at end expiration. Injury to type II pneumocytes contributes to this. Which of the following best explains the alveolar collapse?
options: Surfactant loss raising surface tension
Increased lung compliance from loss of elastic fibers
More negative intrapleural pressure at end expiration
Lower surface tension from excess surfactant secretion
approach: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant, and injury plus protein in the alveoli inactivates what is left.
By the law of Laplace, collapsing pressure equals 2 x surface tension / radius.
With high surface tension, small alveoli have the highest collapsing pressure, so they empty and collapse. The lungs become stiff, and compliance falls.
questions.why: Surfactant, mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, lowers surface tension, especially as alveoli shrink. This keeps small alveoli open at end expiration and lowers the work of breathing. In ARDS, type II cell injury and plasma proteins in the alveoli reduce surfactant function. Surface tension rises, small alveoli collapse, and lung compliance falls, so higher pressure is needed for the same volume. Positive end-expiratory pressure holds collapsed alveoli open. Normally, the inward recoil of the lung and the outward recoil of the chest wall balance at FRC, giving an intrapleural pressure of about minus 5 cm H2O.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of elastic fibers increases compliance and is the change in emphysema. His lungs are stiffer, which is decreased compliance.
A more negative intrapleural pressure would hold alveoli more open, not collapse them.
Excess surfactant would lower surface tension and stabilize alveoli. In ARDS surfactant is deficient and inactivated.

dx: Carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation
case: A 36-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a burning house where furniture and plastics were on fire. She has a headache and is confused. Her temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. There is soot in the nares and oropharynx. Pulse oximetry reads 98% on 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.27 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 25 mm Hg (35 to 45), PaO2 410 mm Hg, and HCO3- 11 mEq/L (22 to 28). Carboxyhemoglobin is 28% (below 3%). Lactate is 11 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). Central venous oxygen saturation is 88% (65 to 75). The diagnosis is combined carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her pulse oximetry reading is 98% despite a carboxyhemoglobin level of 28%?
options: Left shift of the curve raising true oxygen saturation
Dissolved plasma oxygen detected by the sensor
Carboxyhemoglobin absorbing light like oxyhemoglobin
Cyanide raising capillary oxygen saturation at the fingertip
approach: A standard pulse oximeter uses two wavelengths and assumes only oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin are present.
Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs red light much like oxyhemoglobin, so the device counts it as oxygenated.
True oxygen saturation must be measured by co-oximetry, which here would be at most about 72%.
questions.why: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with about 200 times the affinity of oxygen. It occupies binding sites, lowering O2 content, and it shifts the remaining curve to the left so O2 is unloaded poorly in tissues. PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen and stays normal or high, so it gives false reassurance. Standard pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin and overestimates saturation. Methemoglobin, with iron in the ferric state, also impairs delivery and makes pulse oximetry read about 85% regardless of the true value.
whyNot: Carbon monoxide does shift the curve left, but that does not raise the fraction of hemoglobin carrying oxygen. Sites occupied by CO cannot carry O2.
Pulse oximetry measures light absorption by hemoglobin in pulsatile blood. It does not detect dissolved oxygen, which is reflected in PaO2.
Correct.
Cyanide raises venous O2 saturation by blocking tissue O2 use. It does not change arterial hemoglobin saturation or the oximeter's reading of carboxyhemoglobin.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her high central venous oxygen saturation?
options: Inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase
Uncoupling of electron transport from ATP synthesis
Increased oxygen extraction by hypermetabolic tissues
Reduced cardiac output prolonging capillary transit
approach: Normally tissues extract about 25 percent of delivered O2, so venous saturation is about 70 percent. A value of 88% means tissues are not using O2.
Burning plastics, wool, and silk release hydrogen cyanide.
Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome a3 in complex IV, so O2 cannot accept electrons and stays in the blood returning to the heart.
questions.why: Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), the final step of the electron transport chain. Oxygen delivery may be adequate, but cells cannot use it. Oxidative phosphorylation stops, ATP falls, and cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acidosis. Venous blood returns with oxygen unused, so venous saturation is high and PaO2 is normal. Carbon monoxide also binds complex IV, adding to the injury. A high lactate with high venous oxygen saturation after a house fire suggests cyanide poisoning.
whyNot: Correct.
Uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol let electron transport run faster without making ATP, so O2 use rises, which lowers venous saturation. Uncoupling also produces heat.
Greater extraction by hypermetabolic tissues would lower venous saturation, the opposite of her finding.
Low cardiac output gives tissues more time to extract O2, which lowers venous saturation. This is the pattern in circulatory shock.

topics: Inhibitors of the electron transport chain

questions.stem: Considering only her carbon monoxide exposure, which of the following patterns of arterial PaO2, oxygen saturation measured by co-oximetry, and arterial oxygen content is expected?
options: Low PaO2, low saturation, low content
Normal PaO2, low saturation, low content
Normal PaO2, normal saturation, low content
Normal PaO2, normal saturation, normal content
approach: PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen, which depends on alveolar PO2 and lung function. CO does not change it.
Co-oximetry measures the true fraction of hemoglobin carrying O2. CO occupies sites, so saturation falls.
O2 content depends mainly on hemoglobin times saturation, so content falls.
questions.why: Hypoxemia means a low PaO2. Tissue hypoxia means cells get too little usable oxygen and can occur with a normal PaO2. Hypoxemic hypoxia (high altitude, hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, shunt) lowers PaO2, saturation, and content. Anemic hypoxia lowers content with normal PaO2 and saturation. Carbon monoxide is a functional form of anemic hypoxia, but because CO takes up binding sites, measured saturation also falls. Circulatory hypoxia (low flow) and histotoxic hypoxia (cyanide) leave PaO2, saturation, and content normal. Venous O2 tells them apart: it is low in circulatory hypoxia and high in histotoxic hypoxia.
whyNot: Low PaO2, saturation, and content together are hypoxemic hypoxia, from lung disease, hypoventilation, or high altitude. Her PaO2 is high.
Correct.
Normal PaO2 and saturation with low content is true anemia, where less hemoglobin is present but each molecule is normally saturated.
Normal values for all three are seen in histotoxic hypoxia from cyanide and in circulatory hypoxia, where the problem is O2 use or flow rather than O2 carriage.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the rise in her serum lactate concentration?
options: Activation of pyruvate dehydrogenase by excess NAD+
Diversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis
Increased fatty acid oxidation producing acetyl-CoA
Reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerating NAD+
approach: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at complex IV. Without it, the electron transport chain stops, and NADH cannot be reoxidized to NAD+ in mitochondria.
Glycolysis needs NAD+ at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step to continue making ATP.
Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and regenerates NAD+, so glycolysis can continue, at the cost of lactic acidosis.
questions.why: Most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation, which needs O2 to accept electrons at cytochrome c oxidase. When O2 delivery fails (CO) or O2 use is blocked (cyanide), NADH builds up and the NADH/NAD+ ratio rises. Pyruvate can no longer enter the citric acid cycle efficiently, and lactate dehydrogenase converts it to lactate, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can keep making its 2 ATP per glucose. Lactate and H+ accumulate, producing an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Her low HCO3- and the compensating fall in PaCO2 reflect this.
whyNot: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is inhibited, not activated, when NADH is high. Its activity would lower lactate by sending pyruvate into the citric acid cycle.
Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in the liver for gluconeogenesis. This would consume pyruvate and lower lactate.
Fatty acid oxidation needs a working electron transport chain to reoxidize NADH and FADH2, so it slows during tissue hypoxia. It does not produce lactate.
Correct.
